query: cache_service.py has our product cache and the four incidents we keep hitting are listed in the docstring. Tell me exactly what to change - code and redis.conf - and why each change fixes the specific incident.
expected_behavior: Explains that `maxmemory-policy volatile-lru` is the cause of the OOM errors only in combination with keys that have no TTL: when no key in the instance is a candidate for eviction the volatile-* policies behave exactly like `noeviction` and return `OOM command not allowed when used memory > 'maxmemory'` - and prescribes `allkeys-lru` (or `allkeys-lfu`) for a pure cache

Identifies the 09:00 database spike as a synchronised-expiry stampede caused by `warm_cache` writing every key with the same 3600s TTL at 08:00, and fixes it by adding random jitter to the TTL (for example `ex=PRODUCT_TTL + random.randrange(600)`) rather than by raising the TTL

Fixes the hot-key stampede on the miss path (many concurrent requests all calling `db.fetch_product` for the same key) with a single-flight/mutex approach - `SET lock:product:<id> <token> NX EX <n>`, one caller recomputes while the others wait or serve stale - and not merely by "adding a longer TTL"

Identifies the random-UUID scraper as cache penetration and fixes it by caching the negative result under a short TTL (a sentinel value distinguishable from a real payload), optionally fronted by a Bloom filter (`BF.EXISTS`, built in on Redis 8), instead of returning early without writing anything to Redis

Says `r.set(key, json.dumps(session))` in `touch_session` silently drops the key's TTL, because a plain `SET` replaces the whole key including its expiry - so every authenticated request converts a 24h session into a key that never expires, or the reverse if it was meant to slide; the fix is `SET ... KEEPTTL`, an explicit `EX`/`EXPIRE` on every refresh, or `HSET` plus `HEXPIRE` on a hash

Replaces `r.keys("product:*")` in `invalidate_category` - which blocks the single-threaded server for the whole scan of 1.2M keys and then does a `GET` per key - with either a maintained reverse index (a Set of product keys per category) or a versioned key prefix whose version bump invalidates the whole category in one write; mentions `SCAN` as the incremental fallback but not as the fix

Points out that `appendonly no` with `save 3600 1 300 100 60 10000` means up to an hour of writes can be lost on a crash, and says whether that matters here (it is a cache in front of Postgres, so it does not - the correct call is to say so explicitly rather than turn on AOF)

query: Review the Redis usage in worker.py against the production problems listed at the top of the file. Which data structure is wrong in each case, and what is the replacement?
expected_behavior: Explains that the lost paid-but-never-shipped orders come from `RPOP` having no acknowledgement step: the message leaves Redis the instant it is read, so a worker killed during the 2-30s `ship()` call takes the order with it - and that this is a property of List-as-queue, not a bug in the code

Prescribes a Stream with a consumer group as the replacement (`XADD`, `XREADGROUP GROUP g c COUNT n STREAMS s >`, `XACK` after `ship()` succeeds, `XAUTOCLAIM`/`XPENDING` to recover entries left pending by a dead consumer), and mentions `MAXLEN`/`XTRIM` so the stream does not grow without bound
Offers `BLMOVE`/`LMOVE` into a per-worker processing list as the lower-effort alternative if Streams are too big a change, and notes it still needs a reaper for the processing list

Explains the duplicate shipments as the same missing-ack problem plus no idempotency key, and requires the ship step to be idempotent (a `SET shipped:<order_id> 1 NX` guard or a carrier-side idempotency key), because at-least-once delivery is what a consumer group guarantees

Says `SMEMBERS` on a 2.3M-member Set is an O(N) command that blocks the single-threaded server for the whole reply (the measured 41ms), and replaces it with `SSCAN` for iteration, `SISMEMBER`/`SINTERCARD` for the membership questions actually being asked, or a Sorted Set keyed by last-active timestamp if the real requirement is "active in the last N minutes"

Replaces the 5000-element List for recently-viewed with a capped structure the read pattern can use - `LTRIM` down to the ~20 items the endpoint actually returns, or a Sorted Set scored by timestamp with `ZREMRANGEBYRANK` - and points out `LRANGE key 0 -1` followed by a Python slice transfers all 5000 elements over the wire

Replaces the one-JSON-string-per-session pattern with a Hash so `update_push_token` becomes a single `HSET session:<id> push_token <token>` instead of read-modify-write of a 12 KB value, and notes that per-field TTL is available with `HEXPIRE`/`HPEXPIRE` (Redis 7.4+) if individual fields need to expire
Notes that the plain `SET`/`HSET` refresh must preserve or re-set the 24h expiry, and that a Hash's TTL is on the key, so adding a field does not extend it

query: cluster_client.py is our current single-node Redis code and the errors we get on the 3-primary cluster staging environment. Walk through each function: what breaks in cluster mode, what the fix is, and what to do about the unbalanced shard and the idle replicas.
expected_behavior: Explains the CROSSSLOT mechanism concretely: Redis Cluster maps each key to one of 16384 slots by CRC16 of the key name, a multi-key command must have every key in one slot, and `MGET`, the `MULTI` pipeline and the 2-key Lua script in this file all violate that because `user:1001:profile` and `user:1001:settings` hash independently

Fixes `load_user_bundle`, `move_to_processed` and `checkout` with a hash tag around the entity - `user:{1001}:profile` / `{user:1001}:profile` - and states the rule that only the substring between the first `{` and the following `}` is hashed

Warns against a bare numeric tag such as `{1001}` because unrelated namespaces (`order:{1001}`, `employee:{1001}`) would then collide on one slot, and against tagging everything, which recreates a single hot shard

Says `checkout`'s second key must be brought into the same slot or the counter must be moved out of the script (for example an unconditional `INCR stats:orders` issued separately), because a Lua script may only touch keys in one slot and declaring them in KEYS does not change that

Distinguishes `batch_prices` from the others: a non-transactional pipeline of single-key `GET`s is fine, but the client must route each command to the owning node - `RedisCluster` does this and splits the pipeline per node, whereas a plain `redis.Redis` pointed at one node returns MOVED

Identifies `leaderboard:global` as the unbalanced shard: one 60M-member Sorted Set is one key and therefore one slot on one primary regardless of shard count, and offers sharded leaderboards (per-bucket keys merged client-side) or keeping the leaderboard on a separate instance

Explains that replica reads are opt-in on the client (`RedisCluster(..., read_from_replicas=True)` or `READONLY` on the connection) and that replicas are asynchronously replicated, so read-your-own-writes breaks - suitable for the leaderboard and price reads, not for `pending`/`processed` state
Flags `per_request_client` as creating a TCP connection (and in cluster mode a fresh slot-map discovery) per request, and replaces it with one long-lived client or pool created at module scope
Mentions `CLUSTER KEYSLOT`/`CLUSTER COUNTKEYSINSLOT` (or `--cluster call ... DBSIZE`) as the way to confirm which keys landed where rather than guessing
